FG05.question: How does collections efficiency on FY26 invoices differ by distributor tier?
FG05.answer_text: On FY26 invoices, all three tiers show similar on-time collection rates (paid within terms): Tier 2 leads at 33.4%, Tier 1 is close behind at 32.8%, and Tier 3 trails at 30.4%. MH01.question: Why did base-crack warranty claims rise at our Durgapur plant in 2025?
MH01.answer_text: Durgapur (DGP) base-crack warranty claims rose from 543 in 2024 to 695 in 2025, climbing from ~40–50/month in early 2025 to 65–74/month in the May–September peak. The increase is concentrated in a single resin lot, RL-DGP-L2-250310 (line 2, tanks, manufactured from 10 Mar 2025), which alone generated 197 of the 695 base-crack claims in 2025 — the largest contributor by far — with claims starting 10 Apr 2025. The lot_scan anomaly detector flagged this lot as a base-crack outlier, running roughly 4x the expected claim rate (p-values down to ~1e-47) versus 10 peer lots. In short, the 2025 rise is driven by one defective resin lot on line 2 rather than a broad, plant-wide quality shift.

MH04.question: Why does channel stock tend to rise right after each quarter-end?
MH04.answer_text: Channel stock rises after quarter-end because distributors pull forward scheme-discounted purchases to hit quarterly targets, then hold the goods. Across 6,720 complete distributor-quarters, average days-of-stock climbs from 39.7 before the quarter-end window to 42.5 in the 60 days after (a +2.9-day excess), and 28.7% of distributor-quarters are flagged as scheme stuffing. In short, it's scheme-driven channel stuffing rather than genuine demand.

MH05.question: Warranty claim costs were higher in FY26 than in FY25. What drove the increase?
MH05.answer_text: The FY26 warranty-claim cost rose from ₹23.53 M to ₹29.48 M (+₹5.95 M, +25 %), and the increase was almost entirely driven by base-crack failures, which grew from ₹19.34 M (5,848 claims) to ₹24.88 M (6,829 claims) — roughly 93 % of the total cost increase. The base-crack rise was broad-based: all three plants (HWH +₹2.6 M, DGP +₹2.2 M, GHY +₹0.8 M) and all tank SKUs saw higher crack costs, with the 1,000 L and 2,000 L tanks contributing the largest absolute increases. Other failure modes (leak, fitting failure, discolouration) each added only a few hundred thousand rupees and were not material drivers.

MH07.question: Sell-out in Assam jumped in Q1 FY27 (April to June 2026) compared with Q1 FY26. Which distributor drove most of that growth, and what was behind it?
MH07.answer_text: New Biswas Traders (Tier 1, Kamrup Metropolitan, 64 retailers) drove the largest share of Assam's Q1 FY27 sell-out growth, adding 30,807 units year-over-year (56,862 → 87,669). The growth was concentrated in fittings (+23,566 units), led by CPVC Elbow 20 mm (+8,150), Ball Valve 20 mm (+6,700), and CPVC Tee 20 mm (+4,400), plus a new CPVC Male Threaded Adapter 25 mm SKU (+3,000). Pipes also contributed +6,749 units, and the scheme-activity table shows a rate ratio of ~2.4× in both pipe and tank categories in FY27Q1 (vs. zero scheme units in FY26Q1), with a stuffing flag raised—suggesting a promotional push amplified the sell-through beyond organic demand.

MH13.question: Sell-in to distributors jumps in the last weeks of each quarter. Is that real demand, or something else?
MH13.answer_text: The quarter-end sell-in jump is not real demand — it looks like channel stuffing. In the last two weeks of the quarter, sell-in (8.64M units) exceeds sell-through to retailers (7.75M units, ratio 0.897), while for the rest of the quarter sell-through matches sell-in (ratio 1.006), so the spike is inventory building up at distributors rather than being pulled by end customers. This is corroborated by the scheme/stuffing mart: ~29% of distributor-quarter combos (1,926 of 6,720) carry a stuffing flag, and post-window days-of-stock rise (39.7 to 42.5 days, +2.95 excess) while the scheme window's share of sales (0.20) is not above baseline (0.21).
MH13.confidence_note: 9/10 figures traced to query results; untraced: 29%.

AC08.confidence_note: The question could mean more than one thing, so it asks which one you meant instead of guessing.

input.sql:
WITH latest AS (
    SELECT MAX(invoice_date) AS max_date FROM fct_primary_sales
),
bounds AS (
    SELECT 
        make_date((EXTRACT(YEAR FROM max_date))::int, 1, 1) AS this_year_start,
        make_date((EXTRACT(YEAR FROM max_date) - 1)::int, 1, 1) AS last_year_start,
        max_date AS this_year_end,
        make_date((EXTRACT(YEAR FROM max_date) - 1)::int, EXTRACT(MONTH FROM max_date)::int, EXTRACT(DAY FROM max_date)::int) AS last_year_end
    FROM latest
),
periods AS (
    SELECT 
        CASE 
            WHEN p.invoice_date >= b.this_year_start THEN 'This Year (YTD)'
            ELSE 'Last Year (same period)'
        END AS period,
        SUM(p.primary_value_inr) AS total_sell_in_inr,
        SUM(p.qty) AS total_units
    FROM fct_primary_sales p
    CROSS JOIN bounds b
    WHERE (p.invoice_date >= b.this_year_start AND p.invoice_date <= b.this_year_end)
       OR (p.invoice_date >= b.last_year_start AND p.invoice_date <= b.last_year_end)
    GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT 
    p.period,
    p.total_sell_in_inr,
    p.total_units,
    ROUND((p.total_sell_in_inr - ly.total_sell_in_inr) * 100.0 / ly.total_sell_in_inr, 1) AS yoy_change_pct
FROM periods p
CROSS JOIN (SELECT total_sell_in_inr FROM periods WHERE period = 'Last Year (same period)') ly
